{"artifact":"SmeDossierEnvelope","schema_version":"0.4.0","stage_id":"02.dossier_sections","probe":"rdmv-nj-d","lineage":{"input_manifest_sha256":"fe6917441430636a18a3aac4613db6b993a6607d1e1ae4c8a2def24648262bee","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-nj-class-d:lineage:64","source_registry_sha256":"057b72c7c679c997f56ae00ef97a6b14dbe264551f4121b9bf67b0457d9cf7c1","source_liveness_sha256":"1ca7bfbb9e3c0a6b19e5e808ecab6fe8329f3b4799e394abc260d65c1d6513e7"},"envelope_scope":{"kind":"partial_chunk","assigned_section_ids":["C"],"chunk_index":1,"chunk_total":1},"section_char_limit":12000,"sections":[{"section_id":"C","chunk_id":"C.01","merge_seq":1,"domain":"Driver safety appendix: traffic signals, pedestrian signals, sign shapes and colors, warning, work zone, guidance and regulatory signs, and road markings","heading":"C — Traffic signals, signs and road markings: police authority, signal order and meanings, flashing and unlit signals, pedestrian signals, the three sign categories, sign colors and shapes, warning and work zone signs, regulatory signs, the crossbuck and Do Not Enter, and center, lane and edge line markings","learner_facing":true,"markdown":"## C — Traffic signals, signs and road markings: police authority, signal order and meanings, flashing and unlit signals, pedestrian signals, the three sign categories, sign colors and shapes, warning and work zone signs, regulatory signs, the crossbuck and Do Not Enter, and center, lane and edge line markings
Knowledge domain: what each traffic signal, pedestrian signal, sign shape and color and pavement marking tells a New Jersey driver to do, and who can override them.

FACT_ID: sec15-F01 | anchor: A01
A police officer directing traffic can overrule the traffic signals, and a driver must always obey law enforcement orders and directions. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0213]

FACT_ID: sec15-F02 | anchor: A01
Stealing or damaging airport, traffic or railroad-crossing signs or equipment brings court penalties. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0213]

FACT_ID: sec15-F03 | anchor: A02
On a vertical signal, red is always on top, yellow in the middle and green third, with any green arrow at the bottom; on a horizontal signal, red is always on the left. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0214]

FACT_ID: sec15-F04 | anchor: A02
At a red light, stop before the intersection or crosswalk and stay stopped until the light turns green. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0214]

FACT_ID: sec15-F05 | anchor: A02
At a steady yellow light, stop before entering the intersection or crosswalk unless you are too close to stop safely. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0214]

FACT_ID: sec15-F06 | anchor: A02
A yellow arrow warns that the light is about to go from green to red, giving you time to stop safely. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0214]

FACT_ID: sec15-F07 | anchor: A02
On a green light, go ahead but yield to pedestrians and vehicles still in the intersection, and before turning left yield to oncoming vehicles. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0214]

FACT_ID: sec15-F08 | anchor: A02
A green arrow, alone or together with a red light, lets you go only in the direction the arrow points, while still yielding to pedestrians. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0214]

FACT_ID: sec15-F09 | anchor: A02
A flashing yellow light means slow down and proceed with care. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0214]

FACT_ID: sec15-F10 | anchor: A02
A flashing red light means stop, yield to traffic and pedestrians, and go only when it is safe. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0214]

FACT_ID: sec15-F11 | anchor: A02
Flashing red lights at a railroad crossing mean a train is coming, and you may go only after they stop flashing and every other active warning device shuts off. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0214]

FACT_ID: sec15-F12 | anchor: A03
A signal with no working bulbs and no one directing traffic must be treated as a four-way stop. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0215]

FACT_ID: sec15-F13 | anchor: A03
When pedestrians face a steady orange raised palm, they must not step off the curb, and anyone already in the crosswalk will have time to finish crossing. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0215]

FACT_ID: sec15-F14 | anchor: A03
On a steady white walking figure or countdown, pedestrians may cross, and New Jersey law requires turning drivers to yield to them. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0215]

FACT_ID: sec15-F15 | anchor: A03
Signs fall into three categories: warning signs for hazards that are hard to see, guidance signs that identify routes and destinations, and regulatory signs that control speed and movement. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0215]

FACT_ID: sec15-F16 | anchor: A04
A red octagon, with eight sides, is used only for STOP signs. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0216]

FACT_ID: sec15-F17 | anchor: A04
A red triangle, with three sides, is used for YIELD signs. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0216]

FACT_ID: sec15-F18 | anchor: A04
A yellow pennant, a three-sided shape, marks a no-passing zone warning. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0216]

FACT_ID: sec15-F19 | anchor: A04
A yellow pentagon, with five sides, marks a school sign. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0216]

FACT_ID: sec15-F20 | anchor: A04
A white X marks a railroad crossing, and a round yellow sign is the advance warning that a railroad crossing is ahead. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0216]

FACT_ID: sec15-F21 | anchor: A04
An orange diamond warns of construction and maintenance work. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0216]

FACT_ID: sec15-F22 | anchor: A04
Blue rectangular signs give motorist services and information, brown ones point to public recreation and scenic areas, and green ones give direction guidance. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0216]

FACT_ID: sec15-F23 | anchor: A04
When the safe speed on a curve or turn is lower than the posted limit, an advisory speed sign is posted with the warning sign. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0216]

FACT_ID: sec15-F24 | anchor: A04
General warning signs are yellow diamonds with a black symbol or word message. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0216]

FACT_ID: sec15-F25 | anchor: A05
Orange diamond road work signs warn of lane closings, lane shifts, flaggers, uneven pavement and detours, and in New Jersey all traffic fines double in work zones. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0217]

FACT_ID: sec15-F26 | anchor: A05
A flagger has the same authority as a regulatory sign, so a driver who disobeys one can be cited. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0217]

FACT_ID: sec15-F27 | anchor: A05
Regulatory signs are usually vertical rectangles with black wording and border on a white background. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0217]

FACT_ID: sec15-F28 | anchor: A05
A YIELD sign is a white inverted triangle with red wording and a red border inside a white border band. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0217]

FACT_ID: sec15-F29 | anchor: A06
The crossbuck, a white X-shaped railroad sign with black lettering, means the same as a Yield sign, and drivers must always yield to trains because trains cannot swerve. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0218]

FACT_ID: sec15-F30 | anchor: A06
A DO NOT ENTER sign is a white square holding a red circle crossed by a horizontal white band, with the words in white above and below the band. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0218]

FACT_ID: sec15-F31 | anchor: A06
Green national truck signs mark routes and ramps where trucks are allowed, while red ones mark where trucks are prohibited or where designated routes end. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0218]

FACT_ID: sec15-F32 | anchor: A06
Road markings carry the same force of law as signs and traffic signals. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0218]

FACT_ID: sec15-F33 | anchor: A06
Yellow center lines separate traffic moving in opposite directions, while white lines separate lanes moving the same way and mark road edges. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0218]

FACT_ID: sec15-F34 | anchor: A06
A dashed line on your side of the center line means you may pass when it is safe, and a solid line on your side means you may not pass. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0218]

Misconceptions: a dark signal is not a green light, it is a four-way stop; a flashing red at a railroad crossing is not cleared just because the train seems far away; a flagger's signal is not a suggestion, it carries the force of a regulatory sign; pavement lines are not advice, they have the force of law.
Mnemonics: red on top or on the left; eight sides for STOP, three for YIELD and the no-passing pennant, five for school; yellow lines split opposite directions, white lines split same-direction lanes; dashed means maybe, solid means never.
Glossary: regulatory sign means a sign that sets speed or movement rules; warning sign means a sign that alerts to a hazard ahead; guidance sign means a sign that identifies routes and destinations; crossbuck means the X-shaped railroad crossing sign; advisory speed sign means a posted safe speed for a curve below the limit; flagger means a work zone worker who directs traffic.
Dynamic facts: national truck route signage and work zone fine rules can change; confirm them on official New Jersey websites.
